passage:
Subject: sorry, and a real question
Maria,
When Professor Rao tore into our joint poster on Tuesday, I'd shrugged it off by dinner. That's how I am: criticism rolls off, I fix the thing, I sleep fine. So on Wednesday I sent you a cheerful list of edits and a silly cartoon, and I didn't notice you'd gone quiet until Ana told me you skipped the lab meeting. I think I assumed you'd bounced back like I did. That wasn't fair. So, properly this time: how are you doing with it? Not the poster, you. If you want to talk, or just sit in the canteen without talking, I'm free after four.
Chaitanya

qa.q: By when had Chaitanya shrugged off Professor Rao's criticism?
qa.a: By dinner.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya think Maria was feeling after Tuesday?
qa.a: Chaitanya assumed Maria had bounced back and felt as calm as Chaitanya did, so Chaitanya didn't notice Maria had gone quiet.

qa.q: What choice does Chaitanya make in the email?
qa.a: Chaitanya apologises for assuming and asks directly how Maria is, offering to talk or just sit together after four.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt receiving the cheerful list of edits on Wednesday?
qa.a: Maria may have felt more alone, as if the hurt didn't count while everyone else moved on.

grounding: A calm young adult who recovers fast from criticism realises a friend was struggling and asks instead of assuming.

passage: Vasudha asked me last night, "Karthik, how are you never rattled?" Honestly? When I didn't get the internship in June, I was disappointed for one evening, then I made a new list and applied to six more. When the coach yells at practice, I keep the useful bit and forget the volume. That's how I'm built. But I got it wrong with Vasudha herself. Her cousin was in hospital last month, and I kept saying, "It'll be fine, don't overthink." I thought I was helping. She finally told me it made her feel silly for being scared. So now I try something new. I ask, "Do you want solutions or company?" Mostly she says company.

qa.a: For one evening.

qa.a: Karthik thought they were helping, not realising it made Vasudha feel silly for being scared.

qa.a: "Do you want solutions or company?" It lets Vasudha say what she needs instead of Karthik assuming.

qa.a: She felt silly for being scared, as if her worry was not allowed.

grounding: A young adult who bounces back easily learns that a friend's worry was bigger than assumed and starts asking what she needs.

passage: In the college canteen, Irfan's phone buzzed for the fifth time that hour. Vidya: "Are you upset with me? You replied short." He typed "No, just in class" and felt his shoulders sag. He cared about her. But since the exam results the questions came all day: was the dress okay, was he still coming, was her message rude. That evening they sat on the library steps. "I'll always answer the big ones," Irfan said. "But when you're spinning on small ones, could you try your breathing exercise first, or write it down, and then text me if it's still there?" Vidya's eyes filled. "I thought you were tired of me." "Not of you. Of being your only calm." She nodded slowly. The next day there were three texts, not twelve.

qa.a: "Are you upset with me? You replied short."

qa.q: What request did Irfan make on the library steps, and why was it a good choice?

passage:
Usha,
I'm writing this because when we talk about it, you apologise so fast that I never finish a sentence. I love that you tell me what scares you. I want to keep hearing it. But lately I've been answering the same questions ten times a day: did I lock the door, is the landlord angry, did your mother sound cold on the phone. By night I'm so drained I have nothing left to give, even for the big worries. So here's an idea, not a rule. Before you ask me, could you try the walk round the block, or the worry notebook you liked last year? If it's still there after, ask me, and I'll answer properly. I'm not going anywhere.
Mridul

qa.a: The worry notebook Usha liked last year.

qa.a: Mridul feels so drained there is nothing left to give, even for the big worries.

qa.a: Usha could try a walk or the notebook first and then ask; calling it an idea keeps the request caring rather than cold.

qa.q: How might Usha feel reading "I'm not going anywhere"?
qa.a: Usha may feel reassured that the request isn't rejection, which makes the new routine easier to try.

grounding: A partner worn down by repeated reassurance writes with love, asking the other to try their own calming routines first.

passage: Aadhya, I've seen you checking the drawings at midnight. Let me tell you about a young architect I knew, thirty years ago, the worrier of the office. He saw every leaking roof before it leaked. He once stopped a staircase being built because the rise looked wrong by a few millimetres, and he was right. Clients loved him. But he believed every worry meant disaster, and by thirty he was so worn out he couldn't draw a straight line. That young man was me, Ramesh. My senior taught me to ask, "Is this alarm telling me to check, or telling me I've failed?" If it's check, I check. If it's failed, I rest and look again in the morning. Now go home, Aadhya. The drawings will still be here.

qa.a: A staircase, because the rise looked wrong by a few millimetres.

qa.a: He believed every worry meant disaster.

qa.a: "Is this alarm telling me to check, or telling me I've failed?" It lets him check when needed and rest instead of spiralling.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel on realising the worrier in the story was Ramesh?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel less alone and see the worrying as a strength to manage, not a flaw.

grounding: A senior architect tells a junior how his worrying caught real risks, and how he learned to read the alarm as information and to rest.

"Kamal, why are your eyes red?"
"Ma'am shouted at Pinky today. In front of everyone. Her face went all... like this."
"And you cried?"
"In the toilet. I could feel it here." Kamal pressed his chest. "I still can."
His mother, Pallavi, sat down beside him. "You have a big heart. You feel what other people feel."
"Can I make her not sad tomorrow?"
"You can be kind to her. You can sit with her. But her sad belongs to her, beta. You don't have to carry it home."
"Then where does mine go?"
"Tell me, like now. Then we put it down together."
Kamal leaned on her. "Okay. It's lighter."

passage: When I was ten, I cried at every film, even the funny ones with sad bits. When the class bully took Anirban's tiffin, I felt sick all day, as if it were my lunch gone. That night I couldn't sleep, thinking of him hungry. The next morning I brought him two parathas and told the teacher. Anirban was fine by lunch, joking around. I was still shaky. Our teacher noticed and said, "Gautam, telling me was right. But now it's with me, and Anirban's feeling is his, not yours to carry." I didn't understand then. Now, at twelve, when someone else's hurt pours into me, I ask myself: can I do something? If yes, I do it. If not, I let it go back to them.

passage:
Last summer my cousin Sahil kept saying, "Parveen, you're too sensitive," every time I got upset: when he laughed at my drawing, when he popped my balloon. After a while I stopped showing anything. I'd smile, then go and cry in the store room. Ammi found me there one afternoon. She didn't say I was too much. She said, "Of course that hurt. It would hurt me too." Then she taught me something: squeeze my fists hard, count to five, let go, and then say one sentence, like "That wasn't kind." The next time Sahil laughed, I tried it. My voice shook, but I said it. He actually stopped. I don't hide in the store room anymore.
Parveen

qa.a: Parveen went to cry in the store room.

qa.a: Squeeze fists, count to five, let go, then say one sentence; Parveen said "That wasn't kind" and Sahil stopped.

qa.a: He seemed to treat them as a joke, not realising his remarks pushed Parveen into hiding.

grounding: A child called too sensitive starts hiding feelings, and a mother who says the hurt makes sense and teaches a coping tool restores confidence.

passage:
Note for Hemant's parents, from Shreya, class teacher
This week some classmates told Hemant "you're too sensitive" after he got teary during a noisy game of dodgeball. Since then I've noticed a change. He no longer tells me when something bothers him; he goes very quiet and pulls his sleeves over his hands. Yesterday I asked him privately. He said, "I'm trying not to be a baby." I told him his feelings make sense and that feeling things strongly is not babyish. We practised two tools: three slow breaths by the window, and a small card that says "I need a minute" for when it gets too loud. He used the card today. Please tell him the same at home: his feelings are welcome.

qa.q: What does Hemant do with his sleeves when something bothers him?
qa.a: He pulls his sleeves over his hands.

qa.q: What does Hemant's "I'm trying not to be a baby" show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels ashamed of his feelings after being called too sensitive, and is trying to hide them.

qa.q: Which two tools did Shreya practise with Hemant?
qa.a: Three slow breaths by the window, and a card that says "I need a minute".

qa.q: How might Hemant's classmates see him if they watched him use the card calmly?
qa.a: They may understand he just needs a minute, not that he is a baby, which could make teasing less likely.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy hiding his feelings after being called too sensitive, tells him they make sense and teaches coping tools.

"I work better with corrections at the break, not in front of everyone. And can I stand near the side exit, away from the speaker?" Kiran paused, then nodded. That day Nazia was on the beat.
